**PG's answer: don't set out to "start a startup" while you're in school. Keep building the side project, and keep it a side project. If it takes off on its own the way Facebook did, then you have a real decision to make, and running with it may be the right call.**

**Why not now.** He thinks a startup takes over your whole life. Once you start one, you're not really a student anymore, and in his 2014 Stanford lecture he says it flatly: "Do not start a startup in college" [1]. His case is that 20 is not the best age for it. Your early twenties are for diving into projects that seem to have no payoff, and a startup that succeeds takes that freedom away. He says you aren't giving anything up by waiting, because you'll be more likely to succeed later [2][3].

**What to do instead.** Use college to "learn powerful things." In his view the hard part of a startup is the product: knowing what to build and being able to build it. That knowledge comes from fields like computer science, not from entrepreneurship classes. In 2026 he still says to study CS even if AIs end up writing most of the code [4][5]. Your side project counts as that kind of learning, especially if it's something you and your friends actually want. He thinks young founders' own needs predict what everyone will want later, so a project built for yourself is the right kind of seed [6].

**The exception, which he now stresses more.** He has always allowed that a side project can take off without you forcing it, and then "maybe it's reasonable to run with it" [3]. His 2026 essay leans further that way. He points out that Microsoft and Meta both started during reading period at Harvard, and he argues universities should give students more free time for exactly these projects. He still says a running startup is incompatible with being a full-time student, so if yours takes off, you'll have to drop it or drop out [7]. He also thinks the young are the people who can best afford high-risk paths, and that taking risks early pays off [8]. So he's against forcing a startup at 20, not against your project.

**What would change his answer:** real traction you didn't have to push for, like users signing up on their own and friends telling friends. At that point the question becomes "should I run with this?", and he leans toward yes.

**Sources**

2. "though starting a startup could be a good thing to do at some point, 20 is not the optimal time to do it." (Paul Graham, same lecture, 2014-09-30, [18:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1136s))

"You're not sacrificing anything if you forego starting a startup at 20, cuz you'll be more likely to succeed if you wait." / "Then you face the choice of either running with it or not, and maybe it's reasonable to run with it." (Paul Graham, same lecture, 2014-09-30, [21:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1272s))
4. "If you wanna start a startup, what you should do in college is learn powerful things." (Paul Graham, same lecture, 2014-09-30, [30:15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1815s))
5. "Should students still study computer science if AIs will write most code? Definitely." (Paul Graham, How Universities Should Prepare Founders, 2026-08, [link](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html))
6. "usually young founders should make something that they themselves want. You don't have enough experience yet to know what other people need." (Paul Graham, How to Earn a Billion Dollars, 2026-06, [link](https://paulgraham.com/earn.html))

(Paul Graham, How Universities Should Prepare Founders, 2026-08, [link](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html))

Yes. Paul Graham gave a talk in Stockholm in 2026 on this exact question, and his answer was a flat yes: go to Silicon Valley, at least for a while. You don't have to stay forever. He says you can go for a bit and come back, "but you should at least go" [1]. He thinks every field has one center, the way painting had Paris and movies have Hollywood, and for startups that center is the Valley. He thinks that holds even when you have to cross a border to get there [2].

His main reason is the people. In the Valley there are more of them and they're better, so you get more chance meetings with people working on the same things, and he thinks those meetings matter more than planned ones [3][4]. Things also move faster there. Investors decide quickly because competition means good deals get taken, and he says they still earn better returns than European investors [5]. One point bears directly on you: investors outside the Valley tend to assume local startups are second-rate, and that's not just a Swedish problem. Going to the Valley, or just getting into YC, flips that, and investors back home start competing to fund you [6]. He also says the biggest change is in you. In a small pond you can't tell how big a fish you are, and seeing the big names up close turns an impossible goal into a hard one with a clear bar [7][8].

He doesn't say you have to give up on Stockholm. He told that audience the best way to help Stockholm become a hub is to go, then come back with a better startup, Valley money and Valley culture [9]. His suggested way to do that is YC, and he admits that sounds like talking his own book [10]. He's also open about the cost of going home: YC startups that return home are only about half as likely to become unicorns. He discounts that number partly because the founders who stay may simply be more determined [11]. And he notes that money isn't everything. Once you have kids, you'll care more about them than your company [12].

Two things would change the details of his advice, but not the "go" part. If you have a family rooted in Stockholm, he'd accept coming home sooner. If you'd honestly be happy settling in the Valley, the numbers above say staying gives you better odds.

**Sources**

4. "if you're working on something ambitious, there's nothing in the world that's better than serendipitous meetings with people who are working on the same stuff." ([3:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=200s))

One more caveat: he's YC's founder giving this pitch to people YC would fund, and he says so himself. Sam Altman (July 2026) agrees that moving to the Bay Area has been the best way to find co-founders, but says he's less sure of that now than he used to be.

Seibel would tell you to stop. Months of pitching, deck polishing and follow-up meetings is the kind of raise he calls a waste. Investors are probably keeping you around in case you take off, and every hour spent in their meetings makes taking off less likely. Put that time into building, getting customers and growing. Go back out when you have numbers that make investors come to you.

He's been where you are. At Justin.tv he spent about eight months trying to raise. When it was clear the money wasn't coming, the company had two months of runway left, so they worked on making it profitable to survive. He says they got more done in those two months than in all the months of "slinging decks" [1]. He calls a long raise that has "no way it's going to work" "a drag on the industry", and says those founders "would have been way better off" growing the startup [2]. In his view the deck doesn't decide much. When Socialcam was the number two app in the App Store, one of their decks was basically "here's some questions you can ask us" [3]. The investors who now want into his companies told him they chase 80–90% of their deals rather than taking them from the front door [4]. So time spent making investors chase you plays the odds, and "decksmithing" plays against them. In his 2019 MVP talk he made the same point: time on a pitch deck is worth less than building anything you can give a customer [5].

Under all of this is leverage. Leverage comes from the work you do before the negotiation, not from tactics during it. It means bringing more value than you ask for, and being able to walk away when a deal dies [6]. He says the same about sales: a customer doesn't want to feel you need them more than they need you, and investors are no different [7]. Your months of follow-ups are the low-leverage position he's warning against. He would also say that a pile of investor no's doesn't prove the idea is bad. Coinbase took no's on demo day, and if its founder had quit on that signal, Coinbase wouldn't exist [8]. Investors are only one signal; customers are the one that counts.

What would change his answer: if you already have fast growth and investors are coming to you, raise quickly and get back to work. His complaint is with long raises you don't have the leverage to win, not with raising money.

Keep in mind where this comes from. The fundraising episode is co-hosted by Dalton Caldwell, a partner at Standard Capital, the fund that sponsors the show. That doesn't make the advice wrong.

**Sources**

(Seibel, *How Founders Win at Fundraising, Sales, and Hiring*, 2026-10-05, [6:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=404s)). The transcript there gives the eight months of fundraising and two months of runway.
2. "if you just think about how much time is wasted, it's like a it's like a drag on the industry." (Seibel, same episode, [6:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=404s))

Michael Seibel would tell you both to drop the lawyers and settle this within a week. Your cofounder should give back most of his stock, vested or not. Since he's leaving inside the first year, he should keep about 1–2%, or less.

**Why the lawyers are the wrong fight.** Before product-market fit your stock is worth almost nothing. In his words, paying lawyers a lot of money in a cofounder breakup when the stock is worthless "makes no sense" [1]. He thinks fights like this are about ego, not money, and that a lawyer can absorb any amount of anger and "monetize it" [2]. By his estimate, a clean split takes about a week and around $2,000: reasonable severance, clean paperwork, and you each move on [3]. Once you know the partnership won't work, his rule is that the most important thing is to stop wasting time [4]. Each letter your lawyers trade is time and money spent on stock that has no value yet. If you want a mediator, use one, but don't make them the judge [5]. YC's view, which Dalton Caldwell states and Seibel shares, is that it doesn't matter who was right. The aim is a no-fault plan for going forward that both of you can live with.

**Why "I vested it" doesn't settle the equity question.** Seibel says nearly all the value this company could ever create hasn't been created yet. The people who stay will have to create it, so the company needs as much equity as possible to motivate them [6]. A departing founder who keeps a big stake gets a free hedge, and the founder who stays doesn't get one [7]. His numbers apply "even if you vested": get under 5% of the company, and under 2% if the founder leaves in the first year [8]. Elsewhere he puts the first-year range at "1%, 2%, sometimes less than 1%" [9]. At nine months, you're in that range. He often talks to the departing founder first to argue that the equity should stay with the team [10].

**What he'd tell whichever of you stays.** Be generous. Don't act like the victim. Everyone in the company is watching how you treat your cofounder, and being nice costs very little [11]. When one side acts like the responsible party, the other side usually stops acting like a victim too. He'd also remind you that your list of your own mistakes is longer than your list of complaints about your cofounder [12].

**What would change his answer.** If your cofounder broke the law or did something unethical, he says "none of this applies" [12]. His advice also assumes you're before product-market fit and the stock is still worth little. Once there's real value, the stakes are different. And if nobody is carrying the company forward, his argument gets even simpler: there's nothing to fight over, so wrap it up and stop wasting time.

From me, not Seibel: his percentages are what he'd argue for, not legal entitlements. Your cofounder's vested shares are legally his unless your documents say otherwise. Keep one lawyer to paper whatever you agree on. Just stop paying them to argue the case.

**Sources**
1. "in a situation where you're having a co-founder breakup and the stock is worth nothing, paying lawyers a bunch of money makes no sense." (Seibel, *Do You Need a Co-Founder for Your Startup?*, Dalton + Michael, 2026-07-13, [11:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=696s))
2. "a lawyer can suck up infinite amount of your ... anger and monetize it." (Seibel, same episode, [12:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=727s))
3. "Do reasonable severance, sign clean paperwork and and peace out" / "you could do that whole thing in a week and spend like $2,000." (Seibel, same episode, [18:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1119s))
4. "when you really know the probability of success is zero, most important thing is to stop wasting time." (Seibel, same episode, [9:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=566s))
5. "If you're using someone to mediate this, don't make them the judge." (Seibel, same episode, [19:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1186s))
6. "the vast majority of the value this company could create hasn't been created yet." / "you need to make sure that that company has as much equity as possible to motivate the people who are there" (Seibel, same episode, [14:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=887s))

8. "even if you vested, like get down to under 5% of the company, if it's within the first year, under 2%." (Seibel, same episode, [18:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1119s))
9. "After a number of years, 5% typical. Under a year, 1%, 2%, sometimes less than 1%." (Seibel, same episode, [21:22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1282s))

First, a correction: Garry Tan didn't say this. Sam Altman did, at Startup School 2026 (July 2026), while Tan was interviewing him. Altman even flagged that it was a line Tan couldn't say himself: "I can say this, Gary probably can't." [1]

His reason is network effects. Right after saying the gap between YC and second place "has expanded," he calls it "a reminder of the power of network effects." [1][2] He's making that point while talking about co-founders. He says that five or ten years ago, the main thing limiting how many good startups YC could fund was co-founder matching: talented people who couldn't find their people. [3] He met the people he started OpenAI with many years before founding it. [2] So his advice is to get into a network where you'll meet future co-founders as early as you can, because it takes a long time to pay off. In his view YC is now the strongest such network, and the stronger it gets, the further it pulls ahead of the next-best option. He also says YC's once "heretical" rule that founders had to move to San Francisco "was clearly right." He still thinks it's probably good advice, though he admits he has "less of an intuition for it now." [4]

Tan's own part in that talk is smaller but fits the same view. He told the audience that someone in the room would meet a future co-founder there, and he called YC's "loose network," with its habit of helping each other and its long-term outlook, a big part of why it works. [5] But he never claims YC is ahead of everyone else.

Keep the source in mind. This is a former YC president saying it on stage at YC's own event, and his "Gary probably can't" admits the conflict of interest. He didn't give any numbers to back it up.

She didn't say that, and the vault shows close to the opposite. In her 2018 talk "9 Things She Learned From Founding YC," Livingston does use the words "aggressive" and "ruthless," but about **investors** of that era, not founders. She was explaining how YC was different from them.

**What she actually said.** She called early YC "a family" and herself "its mom," "soft and sensitive at a time when investors tended to be hardened and aggressive and I'll throw in ruthless" [1]. She cared whether founders were overwhelmed or eating properly, counselled them on relationships strained by the startup, and helped with co-founder disputes and breakups.

**Who she actually backed.** Her part of the interview was judging character while her partners judged the idea and the technical ability. She looked for four things: were the founders earnest, were they determined, were they flexible-minded, and "most importantly" how did the co-founders get along [2]. She was "very careful about only funding earnest people." If she could tell someone was conceited, YC didn't fund them. She admits YC has funded some conceited founders since, but says that early rigidity is "the basis of the culture" of the alumni network [3]. In 2024 she said the founders she'd known were all "very determined" and independent-minded [4]. So she did want drive, but drive in earnest people, not ruthlessness.

**Why YC worked this way.** It had no LPs (outside investors in the fund), so it owed no fiduciary duty to anyone. In her account, that freedom let YC take more risks on who it funded and "be benevolent to failing startups." That often put YC in conflict with other investors [5]. She also says she still doesn't understand why investors squeeze founders over small outcomes [6].

The one idea in your question that's close to hers is that determination matters. If someone quoted her as saying YC chose ruthless founders, they probably mixed up her description of investors with her description of founders. Your question doesn't say where the claim came from, and these are the only two Livingston talks in the vault. If you have a source where she really said it, send it and I'll check it.

**Sources**
